question.text: A sample of a metal oxide has formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>83</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>00</mn></mrow></msub></math>. The metal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></math> can exist in two oxidation states <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. In the sample of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>83</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>00</mn></mrow></msub></math>, the percentage of metal ions existing in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></math> oxidation state is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>%</mo></math>. (nearest integer)

solution.text:
Let number of ions of M+2=x

Thus, as net charge has to be zero, M+3=0.83-x

⇒2x+3(0.83-x)+1(-2)=0

⇒2x+2.49-3x-2=0

∴x=0.49

%M2+ ions =0.490.83×100=59.03
